Recursion is when a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece of the same problem. Each call does a little work, then hands the rest off to another call of itself, until the piece gets small enough that the answer is obvious and the chain of calls unwinds. A classic example is factorial: n! equals n times (n−1)!, and 0! is defined as 1, which is the simple case that stops the calls. The key is making sure every recursive call moves toward that stopping case, otherwise the function would call itself forever.
